item.title: Norway asks supreme court to overturn environmental verdict against oilfields
item.description: Norway's government on Monday asked the country's supreme court to overturn a lower-court ruling that invalidated permits for three oilfields, in a closely watched case that could reshape how the country approves new petroleum projects.
item.dc:creator: Terje Solsvik, Gwladys Fouche
item.content:encoded: Norway's government on Monday asked the country's supreme court to overturn a lower-court ruling that invalidated permits for three oilfields, in a closely watched case that could reshape how the country approves new petroleum projects. The case pits environmental groups against Norway's oil industry, provider of half the country's export revenue, as well as the government whose policy is to [USN:L8N44I0B4 TEXT:"prolong the extraction"] of crude and natural gas for decades to come. Two lower courts have [USN:L8N3WQ1LQ TEXT:"ruled in favour"] of Greenpeace and Young Friends of the Earth since the two groups first brought the case to trial in 2023, finding that Norway failed to properly assess the environmental impact from the three fields. "If we win this round, it could change Norwegian oil politics forever," Haldis Tjeldflaat Helle, leader of Greenpeace Norway, told Reuters outside the court. "It means that Norwegian politicians will have to actually assess how many lives will be lost, how many forest fires will be created and how much ice will melt due to Norwegian oil." The case concerns Equinor's (EQNR.OL) Breidablikk and Aker BP's (AKRBP.OL) Tyrving and Yggdrasil fields, of which the first two are already in production while the third is due to come on stream next year. The green campaigners argue that the government failed to consider the climate impact of the burning of the fields' oil and gas, known as Scope 3 emissions, and that efforts to rectify this at a later stage were invalid. ENERGY SECURITY AT STAKE, GOVERNMENT SAYS But the lower courts have declined to order a halt to production while the legal process is ongoing, and have also suggested that the government could seek to remedy regulatory shortcomings. "The government's position is of course that the licences are valid," Fredrik Sejersted, Norway's attorney general, told Reuters ahead of the hearing. "If they should be overturned then it will be quite complicated," he said. "Legally, politically and for energy security in Europe." Norway produces around 2% of global oil and became Europe's largest supplier of natural gas after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, making it a crucial provider of energy. The supreme court hearing is set to run for four days, and a verdict in the case is expected sometime later this year.

item.title: Coach carrying German high-school students crashes in Netherlands
item.description: A coach carrying high-school students from Germany crashed in the east of the Netherlands early on Monday, injuring 16 people who were taken to hospital, Dutch police said.
item.dc:creator: Christian Levaux
item.content:encoded: A coach carrying high-school students from Germany crashed in the east of the Netherlands early on Monday, injuring 16 people who were taken to hospital, Dutch police said. Eight of those hurt have been severely wounded and the others suffered minor injuries, the police department of Gelderland province said in a post on X. The coach, which was carrying more than 50 people and was registered in Austria, according to a police spokesperson, crashed near the town of Wezep, some 100 km (62 miles) east of Amsterdam around 4 a.m. (0200 GMT) due to a collision with a delivery van, whose driver was among the injured. The A28 highway was closed in both directions following the accident.

item.title: South Africa's MTN approves $375 million share buyback after profit rise
item.description: South African mobile operator MTN Group said on Monday its board had approved a 6 billion rand ($375 million) share buyback programme as it reported a 21.3% rise in half-year adjusted profit and strong cash generation.
item.dc:creator: Nqobile Dludla
item.content:encoded: South African mobile operator MTN Group (MTNJ.J) said on Monday its board had approved a 6 billion rand ($375 million) share buyback programme as it reported a 21.3% rise in half-year adjusted profit and strong cash generation. CEO Ralph Mupita told journalists the buyback programme would begin on Monday. At 1005 GMT, MTN shares were up 4.61% at 201 rand. Africa's biggest telecom operator, with more than 317 million customers across 19 markets, said adjusted headline earnings per share (HEPS) rose to 793 cents in the six months ended June 30 from 654 cents a year earlier. Reported HEPS, however, fell 5.8%, hit by a 3.9 billion rand non-cash impairment on its 49% stake in Irancell, reflecting Iran's hyperinflation and the sharp depreciation of the rial. Foreign exchange losses in South Sudan also weighed on earnings. The impairment comes as MTN seeks to exit Iran, its last remaining operation in a broader withdrawal from the Middle East. The process has been complicated by U.S. sanctions, in place since May 2018, which have also prevented the company from repatriating about 880 million rand in trapped dividends, Mupita said. "With the sanctions in place, we can't put any money in and we can't take any money out. But if the situation did change in a way where there was a removal of sanctions we would continue with executing our Middle East exit strategy," he added. Outside Iran, MTN's biggest market Nigeria (MTNN.LG) , along with Ghana (MTNGH.GH) and Uganda, helped lift service revenue 17.5% to 115.3 billion rand. Growth in South Africa was 1.5%. MTN said strong subscriber additions and growth in digital and fintech services also supported performance. Core earnings rose 24.4% to 56 billion rand, while the EBITDA margin widened 3.1 percentage points to 47.1%. MTN said the remaining hurdles to its tower deal with [USN:L1N3ZD0JO TEXT:"IHS Towers "]are largely regulatory. It has received conditional approval from Nigeria's competition regulator, which requires it to reduce its stake in the Nigerian business by up to 30% over time at market prices. ($1 = 16.0123 rand)

item.title: Gold climbs to more than three-month high as markets await US inflation data
item.description: Gold rose to its highest in more than three months on Monday, building on gains from last week as a muted dollar boosted appeal, while investors awaited U.S. inflation data and remarks from Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh this week for signals on the interest-rate path.
item.dc:creator: Sukanya Mitra
item.content:encoded: Gold rose to its highest in more than three months on Monday, building on gains from last week as a muted dollar boosted appeal, while investors awaited U.S. inflation data and remarks from Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh this week for signals on the interest-rate path. Spot gold was up 1% at $4,649.08 per ounce by 1004 GMT, hitting its highest level since May 15, while U.S. gold futures rose 0.6% to $4,706.20. Bullion rose more than 5% last week after the U.S. Treasury Department's [USN:L1N44H0P5 TEXT:"buyback support plan"] pushed the dollar lower, making greenback-priced bullion more affordable for foreign investors. "The consolidation of gold prices above $4,600, and the potential for further gains, will depend to a large extent on the U.S. dollar remaining under pressure and Treasury yields stabilizing at current levels or declining further," ActivTrades senior analyst Ricardo Evangelista said. The dollar was pinned near multi-month lows on Monday. Market participants are now awaiting the July Personal Consumption Expenditure price index due on Wednesday and Warsh's speech at the Jackson Hole Symposium on Friday to gauge the policymakers' outlook on interest rates. Traders are pricing in about a 36% chance of a rate-hike in September, with a 64% chance of the Fed leaving rates unchanged, according to the CME FedWatch Tool. Although gold is typically seen as an inflation hedge, higher interest rates tend to diminish bullion's appeal due to its non-yielding characteristic. On the geopolitical front, the U.S. [USN:L6N44K07T TEXT:"threatened"] Iran with what it called "the greatest financial offensive ever marshalled" as it prepared to roll out economic sanctions targeting Iran's trade partners. Yet, oil prices [USN:L1N44K05C TEXT:"slipped"] more than $1 a barrel as investors took profits ahead of an expected announcement from Washington. Spot silver held steady at $68.93 per ounce, platinum gained 0.1% to $1,880.17, and palladium dropped 0.4% to $1,344.35.

item.title: Pro-Palestinian protesters sentenced over blocking Golden Gate Bridge traffic in 2024
item.description: Seven protesters who blocked traffic on the Golden Gate Bridge in a 2024 pro-Palestinian protest against Israel's assault on Gaza have been sentenced to 30 days, with credit for time already served.
item.dc:creator: Kanishka Singh
item.content:encoded: Seven protesters who blocked traffic on the [USN:L1N435033 TEXT:"Golden Gate Bridge"] in a 2024 pro-Palestinian protest against Israel's assault on Gaza have been sentenced to 30 days, with credit for time already served. They were convicted in July of misdemeanor charges by a San Francisco jury that remained deadlocked on the more serious charge of felony conspiracy. Defense attorneys said demonstrators acted out of a moral responsibility to oppose the devastation from Israeli strikes on Gaza and Washington's support for its ally. San Francisco District Attorney Brooke Jenkins said the protest caused a safety risk for those stuck in traffic and there should be consequences when laws are broken. "Throughout history, civil disobedience has mostly involved accepting legal consequences," Superior Court Judge Teresa Caffese was quoted as saying by KQED. "In that spirit, those who blocked the bridge and disrupted the lives of hundreds of commuters should be treated respectfully, but should also be prepared to accept the consequences of their actions." The sentences included half the time in county jail while the remaining days can be served at a work release program operated by the San Francisco Sheriff's Office. There will be four days' credit for previous time already served. The sentencing also included six months of probation, and fines and restitution of over $1,000. The defendants will remain free while the case is appealed, SFGate reported. Defense attorneys argued that protesters resorted to blocking the bridge after writing letters and appealing to congressional representatives produced no result. The jury convicted the seven protesters on misdemeanor counts including false imprisonment, obstruction of thoroughfare, unlawful assembly and in one defendant's case refusal to disperse. The jury did not reach a verdict on the most serious charge of felony conspiracy, an agreement between two or more people to commit a crime coupled with an overt act, which could have had a sentence of up to 15 years. Prosecutors said they will not retry the charges.

item.title: New Zealand to introduce bill banning social media for children under 16
item.description: New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said on Monday his party will introduce a bill in Parliament that seeks to ban children under 16 from using social media, proposing fines of up to 10% of a platform's global revenue for non-compliance.
item.dc:creator: Renju Jose, Alasdair Pal
item.content:encoded: New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said on Monday his party will introduce a bill in Parliament that seeks to ban children under 16 from using social media, proposing fines of up to 10% of a platform's global revenue for non-compliance. The bill would require social media platforms to take reasonable steps to verify users' ages, including by utilising existing account information, facial technology and digital identity documents. "We simply cannot accept the harm being done to a generation of New Zealand children," Luxon said in a statement. "Social media is exposing them to harmful content, addictive technology and pressures they are not equipped to deal with and it's affecting their family life, mental health, sleep and education." It was not immediately clear if the bill would garner sufficient support to pass through Parliament, with one of Luxon's coalition partners, the New Zealand First party, saying it would not support it. "We have been concerned with the proposed legislation and the direction and slippery slope that legislation like this will inevitably take our country," New Zealand First leader Winston Peters, who is also the country's foreign minister, said in a post on X. In December, Australia became the world's first country to ban social media for children under 16, blocking them from platforms including TikTok, Alphabet's (GOOGL.O) YouTube and Meta's (META.O) Instagram and Facebook. That legislation had been a "colossal failure," Peters said, adding that keeping children off social media should be the responsibility of parents. "I won't pretend that it will be simple or that it will be perfect," Luxon said at an event. "We won't get every single child off social media. Some will always find ways around it, but frankly, it's just way too important not to at least try."

item.title: Interventions hold rupee on narrow leash, traders await US sanctions on Iran
item.description: The Indian rupee tip-toed through another lacklustre trading session on Monday as persistent central bank intervention kept the currency trapped in a thin band while investors awaited details of threatened U.S. sanctions on Iran.
item.dc:creator: Jaspreet Kalra
item.content:encoded: The Indian rupee tip-toed through another lacklustre trading session on Monday as persistent central bank intervention kept the currency trapped in a thin band while investors awaited details of threatened U.S. sanctions on Iran. The rupee closed out the session at 95.7450 per dollar, moving inside a range of about 10 paisa through the session. State-run banks were spotted [USN:L4N44L08E TEXT:"offering dollars"], most likely on behalf of the Reserve Bank of India, traders said. Such interventions over the last two weeks have driven the rupee's near-tenor volatility to among the lowest for Asian currencies. The currency's 2-week realised volatility has declined below 2% while the 1-month implied volatility, a gauge of future expectations, has eased to about 4%, below its year-to-date average of 5.2%. "It appears that the central bank wants to deter any appetite to bet against the rupee but whether that is happening will be clear only when intervention recedes," a trader at a Singapore based hedge fund said. The traders expects the rupee to hover between 95.50 and 96.50 in the near-term, with a sustained fall in oil prices seen as key for a meaningful recovery. Ongoing conflict in the Middle East has kept investors uncertain about when supplies from the key producing region could revive to pre-Iran war levels. "We now forecast a more drawn-out Middle East supply recovery, which leaves the market in a deficit throughout 4Q (2026) and 1Q. With that, we revise our Brent forecasts higher, peaking at $100/b in 4Q," analysts at Morgan Stanley said in a note. India imports nearly 90% of its crude requirements, making it one of the world's most vulnerable economies to the Middle East oil shock. Elsewhere, the dollar index firmed 0.2% to 99 while most Asian currencies and regional stock indexes fell. India's benchmark Nifty 50 (.NSEI) was down about 0.3%, faring better than the 1.5% drop in MSCI's gauge of regional stocks outside of Japan.

item.title: Indian food safety officer shakes up Mumbai, one viral raid at a time
item.description: Tukaram Mundhe is an Indian bureaucrat on a mission.
item.dc:creator: Arpan Chaturvedi, Vibhuti Sharma, Dhwani Pandya
item.content:encoded: Tukaram Mundhe is an Indian bureaucrat on a mission. As a state food safety commissioner, the 51-year-old has raided food businesses in the country's commercial capital Mumbai in an unprecedented crackdown on poor hygiene and unsafe food that has captivated the public nationwide. Mundhe has led the suspension of food permits of [USN:L4N44B0ID TEXT:"four Domino's and one Pizza Hut"] outlet in recent weeks, and has also targeted cricket clubs, hotels and well-known restaurants in over 3,000 raids since he took over as Maharashtra's food safety chief in May. When a Mumbai judge accused Mundhe of selective aggression towards private outlets and asked if court canteens were checked, his teams conducted inspections there within hours, shutting some of them which operated without licenses. "Those who try to not comply, they will face what is expected from the regulator," Mundhe said in an interview with Reuters, talking about his no-nonsense approach. "You are dealing with the lives of people." Mundhe has won widespread public admiration across India because he has tapped into deep public frustration. Even though foreign chains such as Domino's (DPZ.O) and McDonald's (MCD.N) are fast expanding, it is local eateries, roadside kiosks and small restaurants — long dogged by concerns over hygiene — that remain hugely popular. Each year since 2020, Indian food inspectors have checked more than 100,000 food samples and found roughly 20% to be unsafe, substandard or lacking proper labels, government data shows. Nearly 8,000 food business licenses have been cancelled in the last three years. "Everyone has tried to normalise this for years by saying it happens in India. It's basically bottled-up anger," said Ankur Bisen, a partner at consumer consulting firm The Knowledge Company. "I have never seen anyone like Mundhe. It's giving people hope." FINDING RATS AND EXPIRED FOOD Mundhe, who is bespectacled and sports a chevron moustache, has an unconventional operating style. He has featured in TV interviews declaring nobody dare bribe him, and that he is not afraid of administrative action despite being transferred numerous times in his 21-year career as an officer of the highly regarded Indian Administrative Service. "I get transferred every year," he said in a 2018 interview. Now, his food safety team's actions go viral daily — raids lead to detailed public statements and graphic images that show interiors of eateries and [USN:L4N44C017 TEXT:"grocery warehouses"] with stained walls, crawling cockroaches and rats, and even expired food — photos that have shocked many Indians. "It was surprising. I did not expect these many violations," Mundhe said. In Mumbai, Reuters visits last week to 25 street vendors and restaurants showed heightened fear about Mundhe's raids. One vendor has swapped artificial red dye for natural chilli in Chinese offerings, while another has started changing his frying oil three times a day and requires staff to wear gloves and head caps. Mumbai's omnipresent street food 'vada pav' — a spicy potato patty in a bun — has not escaped Mundhe's attention. In June, he prohibited use of newspapers as packaging material — often used to wrap the delicacy. Customers are noticing the change and consuming street food more confidently. Supriya Wagle, 14, is happy her favourite vada pav is now being packed in cleaner butter paper, saying that is "surely a relief". CRITICISM AMID CELEBRITY STATUS After finding lapses at some Domino's and Pizza Hut stores, Mundhe's team on Friday suspended the permit of a McDonald's outlet after finding "live pest activity (cockroaches)" and "rotting food". In a statement, McDonald's India said it has "a zero-tolerance approach" to food safety issues and was reviewing the observations. Domino's and Pizza Hut did not respond to Reuters queries. Mundhe's crackdown has included action against a Mumbai British-era cricket club, a 70-year-old ice cream parlour and a 110-year-old Parsi Dairy. He is facing criticism from businesses that say they should be given time to adapt, with some approaching the High Court and accusing his department of high-handedness. In one case, the judges fined his department 500,000 rupees ($5,225) for continued suspension of an eatery even though it improved its compliance. "If there are observations by the court, we take it seriously ... if there is scope for improvement, we improve," Mundhe said. At an event in New Delhi on Friday, fans clicked quick selfies with Mundhe and jostled to shake his hand. One fan told him Prime Minister Narendra Modi should give him a national role. "I don't think I'm a celebrity. I'm just a food safety commissioner," he told Reuters.

item.title: Indian shares fall as investors await details on Iran sanctions
item.description: Indian shares fell on Monday, tracking subdued global markets, as investors stayed cautious ahead of the release of details about likely U.S. sanctions on Iran.
item.dc:creator: Vivek M
item.content:encoded: Indian shares fell on Monday, tracking subdued global markets, as investors stayed cautious ahead of the release of details about likely U.S. sanctions on Iran. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is due to hold a press conference at 1800 GMT on Monday, after threatening to impose "the [USN:L6N44K07T TEXT:"toughest sanctions"] in history" on Iran. In turn, Iran has vowed to shut down all oil exports from the Gulf "if the economic war continues." India's Nifty 50 (.NSEI) fell 0.14% to 24,219.05 and the Sensex (.BSESN) lost 0.22% to 77,369.11. The indexes dropped about 1.3% in the last two weeks, as investors assessed the potential implications of the Middle East conflict on inflation and bond yields. The nearly six-month-old war between the U.S. and Iran has led to a surge in energy prices globally, driving inflation fears. Global stocks slipped on Monday and oil prices eased to $93 per barrel. Eleven of the 16 major sectors fell in India, with the broader small-caps (.NIFSMCP100) dropping 0.3% and mid-caps (.NIFMDCP100) rising 0.1%. Heavyweight financials (.NIFTYFIN) fell 0.4%, while information technology stocks (.NIFTYIT) rose 0.2% in a mixed session. Investors will keep a close eye on the Federal Reserve chief's address at the Jackson Hole Symposium later this week for indications on future rate actions. Gold financiers Muthoot Finance (MUTT.NS) and Manappuram Finance (MNFL.NS) rose 6.2% and 2.1%, as gold prices hit their highest in over three months. Shares of sugar companies extended last week's jump on higher prices ahead of festival season and weak monsoon, while [USN:L4N44L0JG TEXT:"rice-exporters"] gained on strong export demand. [USN:FWN44I0IU TEXT:"Vishal Mega Mart"] (VSSL.NS) jumped 9.7% after re-appointing Gunender Kapur as managing director and CEO. Apollo Tyres (APLO.NS) rose nearly 1% as brokerage firm UBS upgraded it to "buy" from "neutral" on improving earnings outlook.

item.title: Dollar hovers near multi-month lows as debt nerves unnerve investors
item.description: The U.S. dollar hovered near multi-month lows on Monday in a market unsettled by the U.S. Treasury's promise to buy back more long-dated bonds, while traders awaited details of sanctions on Iran and for policy speeches this week in the U.S. and Japan.
item.dc:creator: Tom Westbrook, Johann Cherian
item.content:encoded: The U.S. dollar hovered near multi-month lows on Monday in a market unsettled by the U.S. Treasury's promise to buy back more long-dated bonds, while traders awaited details of sanctions on Iran and for policy speeches this week in the U.S. and Japan. Trade tensions weighed on the Canadian dollar , which weakened 0.5% to C$1.384 per dollar, after Washington imposed [USN:L6N44J03R TEXT:"50% tariffs on Canadian goods"], with Canada retaliating in kind. With the dollar having slid broadly in recent days the euro was trading at $1.1664, down a touch on the day, but in sight of last week's three-month top. Sterling was likewise marginally softer at $1.3627 but near its six-month high of $1.3675 also hit on Friday. The Japanese yen was a touch weaker at 159.21 per dollar. The dollar logged its largest weekly drop against bitcoin in nearly 3-1/2 years on Sunday and it has been sliding sharply on gold over [USN:L1N44H0RB TEXT:"revived fears the currency will suffer"] if the U.S. tries to hold down yields. Long-end yields have been [USN:L1N44F086 TEXT:"climbing globally"] on a combination of a solid economic growth outlook, rising inflation expectations and concern about [USN:L6N44G17Z TEXT:"ballooning sovereign debts"]. Last week, after 30-year yields hit almost two-decade highs, the U.S. Treasury announced it would [USN:L1N44G0GD TEXT:"double buybacks"] at the long end to $4 billion per operation. The size is paltry in a market worth $32 trillion, but the interventionist signal spooked traders and hit the dollar. "The more (U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent) tries to push back, the more markets will push against him," said Marc Ostwald, chief economist & global strategist at ADM Investor Services International. "As a result, you'll see what we've seen in the last week, which is strong support for gold and bitcoin, because of those debasement fears, and people will look to diversify out of G7 bond assets, particularly because they fear that no one's doing anything to rein in the budget deficits." China's yuan , which notched an eighth straight weekly rise last week, hovered near a 3-1/2-year high at 6.7236 onshore yuan per dollar. SANCTIONS AND WARSH Bessent is due to hold a [USN:L6N44K07T TEXT:"press conference"] at 1700 GMT after threatening "[USN:L6N44K07T TEXT:"the toughest sanctions in history"]" on Iran, with markets focused on whether he will target [USN:L6N44H0PZ TEXT:"China"]. Iran's foreign minister has dismissed the threat of new U.S. sanctions as a sign of desperation. Market participants will also be hoping for some clarity on the outlook for U.S. interest rates when Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh speaks in [USN:L6N44H0PG TEXT:"Jackson Hole"], Wyoming, on Friday. He is also sure to face questions about the Treasury's buybacks. "To dramatically alter his communication and provide clearer guidance could risk him being viewed as beholden to the Treasury and hence undermine his credibility. If he sticks to his guns and says little on his views on Fed action, he risks triggering further bond selling," said Derek Halpenny, head of research, global markets EMEA & international securities at MUFG. A Thursday appearance by Bank of Japan Deputy Governor Ryozo Himino will also be closely watched as a prelude to next month's policy meeting. In particular, investors will be looking to see if he pushes back on a shift in market pricing to see a faster pace of hikes.

item.title: Shares, oil dip as US sanctions on Iran loom
item.description: Global stocks slipped on Monday and oil prices eased as investors awaited details of threatened U.S. sanctions on Iran, while the Canadian dollar dipped as a trade war loomed with its southern neighbour.
item.dc:creator: Iain Withers, Wayne Cole
item.content:encoded: Global stocks slipped on Monday and oil prices eased as investors awaited details of threatened [USN:L6N44K07T TEXT:"U.S. sanctions"] on Iran, while the [USN:L6N44J03R TEXT:"Canadian dollar"] dipped as a trade war loomed with its southern neighbour. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is due to hold a press conference later on Monday to outline sanctions on Iran, which Washington says must relinquish its control over the vital Strait of Hormuz. Oil futures were down around 2% ahead of the announcement as some oil traders took profits after big gains last week. , The tech sector was on edge for Nvidia's (NVDA.O) results on Wednesday. Investors are aware how hard it will be for the chipmaker to meet sky-high expectations. "The big news this week will be Nvidia earnings... The tone of that might drive sentiment into the Nasdaq (market)," said Nutshell Asset Management CIO Mark Ellis. Analysts are generally looking for quarterly revenue to almost double to around $92 billion. WARSH SPEECH MAY DISAPPOINT Market participants will also be hoping for some clarity on the outlook for U.S. interest rates when Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh speaks in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, on Friday, though his well-known aversion to forward guidance could lead to disappointment. "There are several reasons to expect to be underwhelmed," said Bruce Kasman, chief economist at JPMorgan, noting that past chairs have not wanted to front-run Fed decisions at the event. "Warsh will rather likely focus on aspects of his 'regime change' agenda," Kasman added. "As the Fed has already been moving toward shrinking the balance sheet, and the committee gave the balance sheet some attention in the July minutes, that might be the most likely topic for him to expound upon." Markets imply around a 40% chance that the Fed will raise interest rates when it meets on September 16 and are fully priced for a move by December. The odds could change depending on what U.S. inflation figures show this week, with median forecasts for core inflation expected to hold at 3.3% in July. Warsh is sure to face questions about Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's surprise announcement last week of at least a doubling in bond buybacks, aimed at restraining a rise in yields that was tightening financial conditions in the economy. His efforts have had little success so far, with 30-year yields at 5.2487% , not far from the recent 19-year peak of 5.3371%. U.S.-CANADIAN TRADE WAR European stocks gained 0.1% (.STOXX) , following declines across Asia including tech-heavy South Korean shares. (.KS11) On Wall Street, S&P 500 futures fell 0.2% and Nasdaq futures were down 0.6%. The Hong Kong-listed shares of [USN:L6N44L021 TEXT:"Alibaba 9988.HK"] slid around 8.5% after the Chinese e-commerce and cloud computing company launched a $10.2 billion share offer and investors worried about returns from its massive AI spending. Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) fell more than 8% after a record $79 billion shareholder-return plan disappointed investors who had expected a larger share of AI-fuelled cash flows. In currency markets, the dollar added 0.5% against its Canadian counterpart to 1.3832 after Prime Minister [USN:L6N44J03R TEXT:"Mark Carney"] said his country would respond to U.S. tariffs with levies of its own as trade talks broke down. Canada will impose tariffs on U.S. steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper products, and electronics, along with some products that the U.S. previously targeted in Canada. The dollar index was up 0.2% to 98.981. The euro dipped 0.1% to $1.1665 after rising 0.9% last week, while the dollar gained 0.1% to 159.13 yen . Gold firmed another 0.9% to $4,643 an ounce , having climbed about 15% for the month so far.

item.title: Oil falls ahead of US announcement of new sanctions on Iran
item.description: Brent crude futures fell to $93.45.
item.dc:creator: Robert Harvey
item.content:encoded: Oil prices slipped more than $1 a barrel on Monday as investors took profits after recent gains and awaited details of expected new U.S. sanctions on Iran , which could further disrupt supplies from the Middle East. Brent crude futures were down $1.55, or 1.64%, to $92.84 at 0911 GMT, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude was at $85.02 a barrel, down $2.04, or 2.34%. Both contracts posted a second consecutive weekly gain last week, rising more than 5%, as peace negotiations between the U.S. and Iran stalled, constraining oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, a route that once carried a fifth of global supplies. "Oil slipped after a two-week rally as traders awaited the U.S. plan to economically isolate Iran due later Monday," said Saxo Bank analysts in a note. U.S. Treasury Secretary [USN:L1N44K02A TEXT:"Scott Bessent"], who is set to hold a press conference at 1 p.m. EDT (1700 GMT) on Monday, has threatened to impose "the toughest sanctions in history" on Iran. President Donald Trump has also threatened to impose sanctions on Iran's trading partners. "Should the pledged embargo be launched, oil supply from the region will fall," said PVM analyst Tamas Varga, adding that the U.S. would likely tighten its naval blockade against Iranian oil exports and that Iran could retaliate with fresh strikes against oil installations in the Middle East. Iran has condemned U.S. plans to announce new sanctions and President Masoud Pezeshkian has called for a [USN:L6N44J01G TEXT:"diplomatic solution"]. Pakistan's [USN:L6N44K07T TEXT:"army chief was visiting Tehran"] on Monday for mediation talks, ahead of the U.S. announcement. Fewer than 20 commodity vessels [USN:L1N44L01G TEXT:"transited"] the Strait of Hormuz at the weekend, shipping data showed on Monday, as Iranian and U.S. blockades restrict traffic through the chokepoint for energy shipments. Offers of Iranian crude to Chinese buyers [USN:L1N44I07T TEXT:"have declined"] and prices have jumped as the U.S. blockade has cut Tehran's shipments, according to trade sources. However, Iran has granted permission for a number of [USN:L1N44J01S TEXT:"Iraqi oil tankers"] to pass through the strait following repeated requests from Baghdad, Iran's state news agency IRNA reported on Saturday. Iraq's SOMO and QatarEnergy both [USN:L1N44L03O TEXT:"offered crude for loading inside the strait "]in tenders, trade sources told Reuters. Brent has climbed back up to around $92 per barrel, from as low as $71 in June, due to inventory draws and a growing sense that Middle East disruptions can last longer, Morgan Stanley analysts said in a note. The bank increased its Brent forecasts, projecting a peak at $100 in the fourth quarter.

item.title: Eli Lilly launches oral weight-loss drug Foundayo in UK
item.description: Eli Lilly has launched its pill, Foundayo, in the UK for weight management and type 2 diabetes, it said on Monday, making Britain the first country in Europe where the oral treatment is available.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Eli Lilly (LLY.N) has launched its pill, Foundayo, in the UK for weight management and type 2 diabetes, it said on Monday, making Britain the first country in Europe where the oral treatment is available. The pill, known chemically as orforglipron, will be available via private prescription after Britain's medicines regulator [USN:L4N4470OP TEXT:"authorised"] the drug on August 10, making it the second GLP-1 tablet to be launched in the UK after Novo Nordisk's (NOVOb.CO) Wegovy pill. England's health cost-effectiveness watchdog, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, must assess the pill before it can become available on the state-run National Health Service. Lilly said it was working with NICE during the agency's assessment of Foundayo for weight management access. Until then, patients can access the pill through private providers. Foundayo will likely be priced between £100 and £120 ($136 and $164), lower than Lilly's Mounjaro injection's £330 price for a month's supply, the company said. Private providers in the UK price the Wegovy weight-loss pill from £74 to £129 per month for initial low doses, with most starting rates tied to multi-month subscription plans. Prices for patients go up as they move to higher doses of the pill. Foundayo remains under review in the European Union, while Novo's Wegovy pill has won a [USN:L4N41Z0VX TEXT:"positive recommendation"] from the European Medicines Agency, with a final decision from the European Commission pending. ($1 = 0.7338 pounds)

item.title: Royals outslug Tigers, polish off 7-0 homestand
item.description: Nick Loftin and John Rave hit home runs as the host Kansas City Royals outlasted the Detroit Tigers 11-7 in a high-scoring affair on Sunday afternoon.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: Nick Loftin and John Rave hit home runs as the host Kansas City Royals outlasted the Detroit Tigers 11-7 in a high-scoring affair on Sunday afternoon. Loftin was 3-for-4 with four RBIs out of the leadoff spot for the Royals, who swept Detroit and finished off a perfect 7-0 homestand, part of an eight-game winning streak. The long ball by Loftin was the highlight of a five-run second for Kansas City. After the Tigers scored four in the fifth to tie the game at 5-5, the Royals added on four more in the bottom of the inning to take the lead for good. Rave had the big hit in the fifth, a 407-foot two-run homer, after RBI doubles by Vinnie Pasquantino and Salvador Perez. All four runs were charged to left-hander Andrew Sears, who was making his MLB debut. John Schreiber (1-3) got the Royals' last two outs of the sixth to earn the win. Sears (0-1) was the bulk pitcher on a bullpen day for Detroit, allowing five runs in four-plus innings. Jacob Waguespack served as the Tigers' opener, tossing 1 1/3 innings and giving up two runs. Detroit's Max Clark had an RBI fielder's choice in the sixth and Ben Malgeri worked a walk with the bases juiced in the seventh. The Tigers loaded the bases in both innings but only managed to trim the deficit in half to 9-7. Kansas City got those runs back with RBI singles by Kyle Isbel and Loftin in the eighth. Royals starter Daniel Lynch IV went 4 1/3 innings, allowing two runs, four hits and one walk and striking out two. The Tigers took their first lead of the weekend on Kevin McGonigle's first-inning RBI double. McGonigle went on to add a fifth-inning homer and totaled three RBIs in the loss. Isbel's two-run single off Ty Madden in the second put Kansas City on top. Loftin did further damage with his sixth homer of the season, a 379-foot, three-run shot to left-center. Clark drew a walk to end Lynch's day with one out in the fifth. Mason Black stepped in struggled against the top of the Detroit order. Javier Baez greeted him with a double, Gleyber Torres scored Clark on an RBI groundout and Hao-Yu Lee added a run-scoring single before McGonigle tied the game with a 392-foot blast to right-center. Kansas City right fielder Jac Caglianone was a late scratch from the starting lineup with ankle soreness. --Field Level Media

item.title: Marlins cruise past struggling Nationals
item.description: Xavier Edwards stroked a go-ahead, two-run single in the fifth inning as the host Miami Marlins completed a three-game sweep with a 6-2 victory over the Washington Nationals.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: Xavier Edwards stroked a go-ahead, two-run single in the fifth inning as the host Miami Marlins completed a three-game sweep with a 6-2 victory over the Washington Nationals. Miami improved to 8-1 against Washington this season. While the Marlins are true National League wild-card contenders, the Nationals have lost 10 of their past 12 games. The game featured a sensational catch by Nationals center fielder Jacob Young in the third inning. On a blast by Heriberto Hernandez, Young ran back and scaled the wall, right foot first and then left. Then while holding on to the chain-link fence with his right hand, Young made the grab and threw to first to double off Otto Lopez. It was less theatrical, but Nationals left fielder Daylen Lile robbed Javier Sanoja of a homer in the sixth inning. Marlins reliever Michael Petersen (3-3) got one out to earn the win. Nationals rookie starter Jackson Kent (0-2) took the loss, allowing three runs and four hits in 4 2/3 innings. Miami opened the scoring in the first inning. Agustin Ramirez drew a walk that featured six foul balls and 11 total pitches. Ramirez then scored from first on Hernandez's line-drive double down the left-field line. Washington tied the score in the fourth. Lile hit a ground-rule double that rolled under the fence in right, and he scored on Dylan Crews' two-bagger that sailed over the head of center fielder Esteury Ruiz. The Nationals loaded the bases with two outs in the fifth, getting a walk and two hit-by-pitches. However, Petersen struck out Abimelec Ortiz swinging at a slider nearly in the dirt. Miami took a 3-1 lead in the bottom of the fifth on a rally that started with none on and two outs. Edwards got the big hit - a bases-loaded, two-run single. Washington cut its deficit to 3-2 in the sixth as Keibert Ruiz walked and scored from first on Jorbit Vivas' two-out double off the wall. Marlins right fielder Griffin Conine crashed into that wall and fell to the ground in pursuit of that hit. Miami extended its lead to 5-2 in the bottom of the sixth on pinch-hitter Joe Mack's RBI double down the left-field line and Lopez's sacrifice fly to shallow right field. Mack added an RBI groundout in the eighth. --Field Level Media

item.title: Mediator Pakistan to hold talks in Iran on US 'economic D-Day'
item.description: Pakistan's army chief was visiting Tehran on a mediating mission as the United States prepared to roll out "the greatest financial offensive ever" targeting Iran's trade partners.
item.dc:creator: Menna Alaa El-Din, Asif Shahzad, Ariba Shahid
item.content:encoded: Pakistan's army chief was visiting Tehran on a mediating mission on Monday as the United States prepared to roll out "the greatest financial offensive ever" targeting Iran's trade partners. Iran dismissed the U.S. threat, vowing to shut down all oil exports from the Gulf "if the economic war continues". It issued a [USN:L1N44L07X TEXT:"new warning to shipping"] not to pass through the Strait of Hormuz without its permission, listing 45 ships it said had violated its rules and threatening retaliation for any ship-to-ship transfers with them. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has promised to reveal severe measures on Iran, which has endured near-continuous economic sanctions since the Islamic Revolution of 1979, when he gives a press conference at 1 p.m. EDT (1700 GMT) on Monday. "At dawn begins an economic D-Day — the single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary," Bessent wrote in an opinion piece published in the Financial Times on Sunday. Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir, who has built a [USN:L1N44L090 TEXT:"personal rapport"] with U.S. President Donald Trump, arrived in Iran on Monday for talks, Iranian media said. Pakistan said the visit was part of its efforts "to promote regional peace and stability", and a Pakistani source said Munir was expected to meet people close to Iran's supreme leader. PROJECTILE HITS TANKER NEAR SAUDI RED SEA PORT, MONITORS SAY Two Pakistani sources said Trump had called Munir last week, with another saying the main request was to [USN:L1N44L090 TEXT:"bring Iran back to negotiations"]. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The U.S. and Iran have not conducted air strikes on each other's militaries for weeks, but their last official face-to-face talks to end the six-month-old conflict took place in June and strikes on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz have continued. A projectile [USN:L1N44L08M TEXT:"struck a tanker"] west of the Saudi port city of Yanbu in the Red Sea on Monday, causing a fire on the main deck, shipping monitors from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said. They did not say who had launched the projectile. Iran's Houthi allies last month [USN:L1N43M0DO TEXT:"said they would block"] Saudi oil exports diverted to the Red Sea to avoid Hormuz. Thousands of people have died, most of them in Iran and Lebanon, since the U.S. and Israel began strikes on February 28, degrading much of Iran's conventional military capacity and inflicting economic pain while killing [USN:L6N43B0GV TEXT:"Iran's then-Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei"]. Yet Iran has preserved enough missile and drone capability to attack its Gulf neighbours and bring shipping in the Strait of Hormuz to [USN:L1N44L01G TEXT:"a near standstill"], pushing up world fuel prices. The exact state of Iran's nuclear program, which the Americans and Israelis aim to wipe out, remains unknown. Oil prices [USN:L1N44K05C TEXT:"eased"] on Monday after two weeks of gains as investors took profits ahead of the expected U.S. announcement. Without detailing specific measures, Bessent signalled the U.S. would target "fearful nations" that practice "appeasement" by engaging with Iran's economy and financial system. "They would do well to consider the consequences of sustaining it," he wrote in the Financial Times. Iran has been bracing for the sanctions for days, issuing a series of statements hinting at a major military response. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, on Sunday suggested economic retaliation. "If the economic war continues, not a single drop of oil will be exported, neither through the Strait of Hormuz nor from anywhere in the Persian Gulf," Rezaei wrote in a social media post. "Iran will regard any country’s participation in or support for America’s economic war against the Iranian people as an act of war." CHINA SAYS SANCTIONS AND PRESSURE TACTICS WILL NOT WORK Bessent [USN:L6N44H0X1 TEXT:"previously urged China"] to cooperate with the U.S. China has been the biggest buyer of Iranian oil for several years, although the U.S. blockade of Iran's ports, renewed in mid-July, has already [USN:L4N44L0FN TEXT:"cut Iranian oil flows to China"]. The Chinese foreign ministry said sanctions and pressure tactics do not help and that Beijing would do what was necessary to protect China's interests. Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi dismissed the latest moves from Washington, which has said the measures will bring down the Iranian government, saying that successive such declarations by the United States had come to nothing. Though Tehran remains outwardly defiant, Iranian officials who spoke to Reuters [USN:L1N44F051 TEXT:"have expressed concern"] that further economic punishment could increase hardships, reignite unrest and further erode the Islamic Republic's legitimacy. Iran entered the war with high inflation, energy shortages and deep structural weaknesses, and must now contend with disrupted trade, lost production and the cost of rebuilding damaged infrastructure. A slide in the rial currency, which prompted protests in January that were violently suppressed, [USN:S8N42206W TEXT:"reached a new record low"] on Monday, 25% below its January level.

item.title: Iran says new sanctions threatened by 'desperate' US will fail
item.description: Iran's economy is under huge pressure from sanctions and thousands have died in airstrikes since February.
item.dc:creator: Elwely Elwelly, Menna Alaaeldin
item.content:encoded: Iran's foreign minister dismissed the threat of new U.S. sanctions as a sign of desperation on Sunday and said the expected new measures would fail to defeat Tehran. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who is due to hold a press conference at 2 p.m. EDT (1800 GMT) on Monday, has threatened to impose "[USN:L6N44H0X1 TEXT:"the toughest sanctions in history"]" on Iran. Iran's economy is already under huge pressure from international sanctions, its infrastructure has been hit repeatedly and thousands of people have been killed in airstrikes on the Islamic Republic since the U.S. and Israel launched attacks on February 28. But Tehran remains defiant after nearly six months of war and has brought shipping to a virtual standstill in the Strait of Hormuz, refusing to allow unauthorized oil tankers to transit a waterway that is vital for global oil shipments. The effective blockade of the strait has pushed up [USN:L1N44I027 TEXT:"global oil prices"]. Describing what he said were "repetitive scenarios", Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said in a video posted on Telegram: "The fact that they (U.S. leaders) have moved on from military operations ... to bring up the same old plans shows that they are desperate." He said Washington must speak to Iran respectfully to find "a solution based on justice and honour." "We have never been afraid. All of their actions - whether blockades or other military moves they have made - have failed, and this new issue of theirs will fail as well," he said. U.S. President Donald Trump has warned of economic consequences against any country that provides "any type of lifeline to Iran" and Bessent has urged cooperation with Washington by [USN:L6N44H0PZ TEXT:"China"], which buys more than 80% of Iran's shipped oil, according to 2025 data from analytics firm Kpler. China has urged diplomacy. PAKISTAN'S ARMY CHIEF TO VISIT TEHRAN Iran said [USN:L1N44K01W TEXT:"Pakistan's army chief"], Asim Munir, would visit Tehran on Monday as part of efforts to restore peace and security in the region, but gave few details. Pakistan has been mediating in the conflict and a Pakistani government source said Munir would touch on recent developments including the U.S. threat of new sanctions. Trump said on Friday that Washington was observing "what happens" in the conflict. "They would love to make a deal, but they're not ready to make the right deal, in my opinion," Trump said of Iran. U.S. attacks have severely diminished Iran's economy and devastated its navy and air force, but Tehran maintains enough missile and drone capability to impede oil tanker traffic and attack regional rivals. Iranian Parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said on Saturday that Tehran had received "numerous messages" from neighbouring countries about establishing new regional security arrangements and economic cooperation. Qalibaf did not say which countries he was referring to. He accused the U.S. of endangering the security of its allies in the region for the sake of Israel, adding that an independent, "homegrown" regional order would deliver peace and security. Trump has yet to achieve objectives he set at the start of the war such as dismantling Iran's nuclear programme — the state of which remains uncertain given that U.N. inspectors have been shut out since 2025 — and creating conditions for Iranians to overthrow their clerical rulers. While Iran remains defiant, President Masoud Pezeshkian has also called for a diplomatic solution. "It would be better to end the war today, when we are powerful and have dignity, and the whole world acknowledges our victory and emphasizes that America, contrary to all regulations, attacked our schools, hospitals, and infrastructure and is hated in the world," the ISNA news agency quoted him as saying on Friday.

item.content:encoded: Les valeurs à suivre à Wall Street Principales valeurs à suivre lundi à Wall Street, où les contrats à terme sur les principaux indices suggèrent une ouverture stable (-0,01%) pour le Dow Jones <.DJI>, en baisse de 0,12% pour le Standard & Poor's-500 <.SPX> et de 0,49% pour le Nasdaq. Jackson Hole: Le premier discours de Warsh sous surveillance avec l'agitation sur l'obligataire WASHINGTON, 24 août (Reuters) - Le discours de Kevin Warsh, président de la Réserve fédérale américaine (Fed), lors de la conférence de Jackson Hole qui débute cette semaine, suscitera sans aucun doute un intérêt allant bien au-delà de l'évidence, à un moment où le marché cherche des éclaircissements sur la récente flambée des rendements obligataires et des garanties quant à l'indépendance de la banque centrale. Le milliardaire allemand Klaus-Michael Kuehne s'éteint à l'âge de 89 ans Le milliardaire allemand Klaus-Michael Kuehne, actionnaire majoritaire du groupe logistique suisse Kuehne+Nagel, est décédé à l'âge de 89 ans, a annoncé lundi la société. Volkswagen: Les salariés inquiets de la communication du directoire BERLIN, 24 août (Reuters) - Les salariés de Volkswagen ont critiqué ce qu’ils ont qualifié de "communication externe désastreuse" de la part du directoire, alors que le plus grand constructeur automobile européen envisage de nouvelles réductions de coûts, selon un article interne du comité d’entreprise consulté lundi par Reuters. Shein pourrait atteindre une valorisation de $27 mds lors de son IPO à Hong Kong HONG KONG, 24 août (Reuters) - La valorisation de Shein a chuté d'environ 70% par rapport au pic de près de 100 milliards de dollars atteint lors d'un tour de table effectué il y a quatre ans, alors que le géant en ligne chinois de la mode éphémère entend lever jusqu'à 1,77 milliards de dollars en vue de son introduction en Bourse à Hong Kong. Shell: Les actifs chimiques américains suscitent l'intérêt d'Exxon et LyondellBasell selon le Financial Times 24 août (Reuters) - Shell a suscité l'intérêt de plusieurs acquéreurs potentiels, dont ExxonMobil et LyondellBasell, pour ses actifs chimiques américains, qui pourraient atteindre une valeur de 8 milliards de dollars (6,85 milliards d'euros), a rapporté lundi le Financial Times (FT). Le Vatican va construire une centrale agrivoltaïque à €100 mlns - sources Le Vatican va construire une centrale agrivoltaïque qui pourrait alimenter le Saint-Siège en électricité d'origine renouvelable d'ici deux ans, ont déclaré des sources impliquées dans les discussions sur le projet. Zone euro: Légère amélioration surprise de la confiance des consommateurs en août La confiance des consommateurs de la zone euro s'est légèrement améliorée depuis le début du mois d'août, montrent vendredi les résultats préliminaires de l'enquête mensuelle de la Commission européenne. Etats-Unis: Baisse des inscriptions au chômage à 206.000 Les inscriptions au chômage ont baissé de façon inattendue aux Etats-Unis, à 206.000, lors de la semaine au 15 août, a annoncé jeudi le département du Travail. GB-PMI: Le secteur des services reprend de la vigueur en août L'activité du secteur des services britannique, moteur de l’économie du pays, a connu une reprise inattendue en août, qui vient s’ajouter aux signes de résilience observés outre-Manche malgré le conflit au Moyen-Orient, selon une enquête publiée vendredi.

item.content:encoded: Football: Des fans du SC Cambuur blessés par des feux d'artifice lancés par des supporters du Feyenoord AMSTERDAM, 24 août (Reuters) - Le club néerlandais du SC Cambuur a indiqué que des supporters avaient subi des brûlures, des lésions auditives et des blessures aux yeux après que des supporters du Feyenoord en déplacement ont lancé des feux d'artifice lors du match de championnat disputé dimanche à Leeuwarden. Doublé mondial historique pour le badminton français Le badminton français a remporté dimanche à New Delhi les deux premiers titres mondiaux de son histoire. Tennis: Blessé, le N°1 mondial Jannik Sinner forfait pour l'US Open Le numéro un mondial Jannik Sinner a déclaré forfait pour l'US Open (23 août-13 septembre) à cause d'une douleur persistante au genou droit, a indiqué vendredi le joueur italien de 24 ans. Cyclisme-Le double champion du monde Julian Alaphilippe annonce sa retraite Double champion du monde de cyclisme sur route en 2020 et 2021, Julian Alaphilippe (34 ans) a annoncé vendredi sur ses réseaux sociaux son départ à la retraite. F1: Verstappen prolonge avec Red Bull jusqu'à fin 2030 Max Verstappen a prolongé jeudi son contrat avec Red Bull jusqu'à la fin de la saison 2030, mettant fin aux spéculations sur l'avenir à court terme du quadruple champion du monde de Formule 1. La match PSG-Stade Rennais inversé en raison de l'état de la pelouse du Parc des Princes La Ligue de football professionnel (LFP) a annoncé que la rencontre opposant le champion en titre le Paris Saint Germain et le Stade Rennais, initialement prévue dimanche au Parc des Princes à Paris, se jouerait finalement au Roazhon Park de Rennes en raison de l'état de la pelouse du stade parisien. Cyclisme: Pogacar à l'assaut de la Vuelta, le dernier grand tour qui manque à son palmarès Moins d'un mois après avoir conquis son cinquième Tour de France, record égalé, Tadej Pogacar sera samedi au départ de la Vuelta pour tenter de remporter le seul grand tour qui manque encore à son palmarès pourtant déjà largement garni. Football: La Ligue 1 reprend ses droits après une valse des entraîneurs inédite L'Olympique de Marseille reçoit le RC Strasbourg vendredi en ouverture de la saison 2026-2027 de Ligue 1, deux équipes qui ont changé d'entraîneur, comme un symbole de la valse des coachs qui a eu lieu cet été, tandis que le Paris Saint-Germain, toujours sous la houlette de Luis Enrique, visera un sixième titre consécutif. Football : une association de défense des droits exhorte la FIFA à bloquer la candidature d'Infantino à sa réélection L'organisation de défense des droits de l'homme FairSquare a exhorté la FIFA à déclarer Gianni Infantino inéligible à un nouveau mandat de président, arguant qu'il a déjà exercé le nombre maximal de trois mandats autorisés par les statuts de l'instance. Volley: L'équipe de France féminine veut confirmer à l'Euro après un Mondial historique L'équipe de France féminine lance son championnat d'Europe vendredi face à la Slovaquie avec l'objectif de confirmer sa progression récente entrevue lors du Mondial de l'an passé, où elle avait atteint un quart de finale inédit.
